Class OidcTokenEndpoint

java.lang.Object
iu.oidc.provider.OidcTokenEndpoint
public class OidcTokenEndpoint extends Object
Answers the OAuth 2.0 token request.

Nothing here is a servlet. It takes a request, reports what came of it, and leaves the transport to write the response.

Client authentication

Every request authenticates its client through ClientAuthenticator. A registration's shape decides which method it may use, so a client cannot pick a weaker one than it was registered for. Credentials belong to endpoints: when a request supplies redirect_uri, only an endpoint registering that exact URI is eligible; when it supplies resource — which RFC 8707 permits naming more than once — only an endpoint registering every named resource URI is eligible, an endpoint's own resource with no URI counting as this provider's own issuer identifier for that comparison. If both selectors are supplied they must match the same endpoint. A request supplying neither tries each endpoint in turn, since not every token request has either selector. Naming a resource no endpoint registers is refused as invalid_target, distinct from invalid_client: the client may be perfectly able to authenticate, it simply asked for a target this provider doesn't recognize.

Grant types

  • client_credentials acts for the client itself. There is no end user, so no ID token is issued and openid is not granted; the scope comes from the resources the authenticating endpoint registers for the named resource, narrowed to a requested scope when one is given. Naming no resource doesn't restrict this to the endpoint's own entry: every resource whose scope overlaps a requested scope is considered, so a client need not name a resource it can identify by the scope it's asking for.
  • authorization_code redeems a code OidcAuthorizeEndpoint issued. The code resolves a grant through GrantStore, and the request must repeat the redirect_uri it was issued to and satisfy the PKCE challenge it recorded.
  • refresh_token redeems a refresh token this endpoint issued, which is a GrantStore reference of its own kind carrying the same grant. Each redemption spends the old reference and, so long as offline_access is still granted and the original authentication hasn't aged past the deployment's refresh token time to live, issues a new one good for whatever of that lifetime remains — so a session can be kept alive by refreshing, but never beyond the age its authentication was good for in the first place.

Whichever grant type answers, the access token's audience is derived from the granted scope: every registered resource whose scope was granted. A resource with no URI names this provider's own issuer identifier, so a scope such as openid only addresses a token to this provider when a resource registers that scope for it; nothing is added on the strength of a scope alone, and a scope with no registered resource behind it contributes no audience at all rather than falling back to the issuer implicitly. For authorization_code and refresh_token, that derivation is bounded by whatever resource the authorization endpoint recorded when the code was first issued; a resource repeated at redemption may narrow the audience to a subset of that, but naming one never authorized is refused as invalid_target rather than silently widening it. This is separate from a GrantStore reference's own aud claim, which always names this provider — that token is never read by anything but the endpoint that wrote it.

Identity, roles, and impersonation

A code or refresh grant answers for whoever the identity provider authenticated, unless the authorization request named an impersonated principal the authenticated principal holds a backdoor role for and this deployment isn't a production one — in which case the impersonated principal is who the tokens answer for instead, and the real principal rides along as the act claim. Either way, the effective principal must hold one of the endpoint's access roles to get a token at all, and the application roles it matches are added as claims to both the access token and the ID token.

Claims follow scope

What an ID token says about its subject is decided the same way a UserInfo response is: the granted scope admits a set of claims, deny-by-default, and the claims source is asked for those and no others. A client that asks for openid alone gets an ID token naming a subject and nothing else about them.

  • Constructor Details

    • OidcTokenEndpoint

      public OidcTokenEndpoint(edu.iu.oidc.config.IuOidcProviderReference reference)
      Creates a token endpoint.

      The data store is read once, here, since an endpoint cannot usefully outlive it. Everything else is read per request, so a configuration change — including whether this is a production deployment — takes effect on the next one.

      Parameters:
      reference - application resources this provider's endpoints read through
